239.title: Who moves the mind?
239.hook: a student asks who moves the mind; the Kena answers: Brahman
239.carry: brahman is the one the mind runs on
239.howItsDone: The Kena's opening question, 'kena?', by whom?, is a classic starting point for self-inquiry in Vedanta. Many Hindus say the Gayatri mantra each morning; its last line asks the divine light to move, or inspire, our minds.

segments.voice: Last week, the whole Isha in eighteen verses, ending with hiranmaya: the face of truth covered with gold. Your line: uncover it, so I may see.

Long ago, a student sat down near his teacher. That's one old meaning of the word Upanishad: sitting down near. He didn't ask for a blessing or a rule. He asked the question small children ask in bed, right before grown-ups teach them to stop: who's thinking my thoughts? The teacher didn't laugh it off. He answered, and the answer became a whole Upanishad, named after the student's first word. Kena. By whom?
screen: `A STUDENT SITS DOWN NEAR.` → `WHO'S THINKING MY THOUGHTS?` → `KENA: BY WHOM?`

segments.voice: Here is the question, the first verse. By whom willed, by whom sent, does the mind fly out to its objects? By whom commanded does the first breath move? By whom impelled do people speak? What god sets the eye and the ear to work? Mind, breath, speech, eye, ear: the things you'd call you. And notice: you didn't order your next thought. It arrived. You don't decide to breathe; it breathes. So who is doing the doing? The teacher's answer, unfolding all week, is one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: Brahman. You've met the word. It's the tradition's name for the ultimate reality, the ground of everything. And the Kena says Brahman isn't far off, past the sky. It's the one your mind runs on, so close the mind can't grab it, the way a hand can't grab itself. This isn't only for philosophers. Many teachers hear the same idea in the prayer you met on day three, the Gayatri, which many Hindus say every morning. Its last line asks the divine light: may it move our minds, may it set our thinking going. The Kena asks: by whom is the mind sent out? The Gayatri asks that light, at sunrise, to be the one who sends it. So on the nights a mind won't stop, the Hindu answer isn't only: calm down. It's: your racing mind isn't the boss here. Something deeper moves it, and you can ask that something to steer.
screen: `BY WHOM DOES THE MIND FLY OUT?` · `WHO IS DOING THE DOING?` · `BRAHMAN: WHAT THE MIND RUNS ON.` · `GAYATRI: MAY IT MOVE OUR MINDS.` · then, large: `BRAHMAN IS THE ONE THE MIND RUNS ON.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and wait for the next thought without making one. When it comes, notice you didn't order it; it arrived. If you pray, say the Gayatri's meaning softly: may the light move my mind. If you don't, hold the Kena's question instead, not to answer it, just to hold it: by whom? Rest in the gap between thoughts.
Kena, by whom? The question that opens this Upanishad: by whom does the mind fly out to its objects, by whom does the first breath move?
Your line: brahman is the one the mind runs on. Tomorrow the teacher answers. See you then.

240.title: The ear of the ear
240.hook: the teacher answers: behind every sense is the self, the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind
240.carry: the atman is the ear of the ear
240.tomorrow: The eye does not go there
240.howItsDone: In Vedanta teaching, Kena 1.2 ('the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind') is often used to point students toward awareness itself as distinct from what it perceives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kena: by whom does the mind fly out? Your line: brahman is the one the mind runs on.

In a dark movie theater, a whole film goes by, the car chase, the kiss, the explosion, and nobody in the seats looks at the light. But without the projector's beam, there's nothing on the screen at all. Every image is made of it, and it's the one thing nobody watches. Yesterday the student asked who moves the mind. Today the teacher answers, and his answer sounds like a riddle. It's really a description of that light.
screen: `THE MOVIE AND THE LIGHT.` → `THE ONE THING NOBODY WATCHES.` → `THE TEACHER ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Verse two. It is the ear of the ear. The mind of the mind. The speech of speech. The breath of breath. The eye of the eye. Shrotrasya shrotram: the hearing of hearing. What does that mean? Your ear hears sounds, but something is aware of the hearing itself: something knows that you are hearing. That's the ear of the ear. Your mind thinks thoughts; something is aware of the thinking. That's the mind of the mind. The Kena points past each sense to the awareness it runs on, the way you'd point past the picture to the light. Hindu teachers have a name for that listener in you: the atman, your truest self, sometimes called the sakshi, the witness. The verse adds that the wise, letting go of the idea that the senses are all there is, go beyond this world and become deathless. Here's where it lands. People usually identify with what's on the screen. I'm angry. I'm tired. I'm this worry. The Kena says the anger is a picture; you're closer to the light it's shown in. That doesn't make the anger fake, and it doesn't mean you shouldn't deal with it. It means there's a place in you the anger doesn't reach. The atman, the ear of the ear, isn't hurt by a harsh word. It just hears it. Vedanta schools explain this light differently. The Kena's point is that it's here: not far away, not somewhere you travel to, but behind every single thing you notice today.
screen: `THE EAR OF THE EAR.` · `THE MIND OF THE MIND.` · `ATMAN: THE WITNESS IN YOU.` · `A PLACE THE ANGER DOESN'T REACH.` · then, large: `THE ATMAN IS THE EAR OF THE EAR.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and listen to the sounds around you, a fan, traffic, your own breath, and let them come. Then, instead of the sounds, notice the hearing itself, something aware that sound is happening, and rest there for a few breaths. If a thought pulls you away, notice that something is aware of the thought too, and come back to the listening.
Shrotra, the ear, hearing. It is the ear of the ear, shrotrasya shrotram: something is aware of the hearing itself, the mind of the mind, the breath of breath.
Your line: the atman is the ear of the ear. There is a listener behind the listening. Day two hundred forty, done.

241.title: The eye does not go there
241.hook: the eye cannot go there, nor speech, nor the mind
241.carry: the image points; brahman is the one who sees
241.howItsDone: Hindus who study Vedanta often learn the Kena's refrain (1.4–1.8) as a teaching that Brahman is the knower, never an object known, alongside continuing worship of God in images and names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, shrotra: it is the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind. Your line: the atman is the ear of the ear.

Nobody has ever seen their own eyes. A mirror shows a picture of them. The actual eyes, the ones doing the seeing, stay out of sight: the one thing in the field of vision that can never be in the field of vision. A tongue can't taste itself either. The Kena's next verses start from this puzzle. If Brahman is the eye of the eye, the eye will never see it. And then the text says something that sounds almost shocking for a sacred book.
screen: `NOBODY SEES THEIR OWN EYES.` → `THE ONE THING NEVER IN VIEW.` → `A SHOCKING LINE.`

segments.voice: Verse three: the eye does not go there, nor speech, nor the mind. We don't know it; we don't understand how anyone could teach it. It is other than the known, and beyond the unknown. So we have heard from the ancients who explained it to us. The teacher can't hand this over like an object. Then, in verses four to eight, a refrain comes five times. That which speech cannot express, but by which speech is expressed: know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here. That which the mind cannot think, but by which the mind thinks. That which the eye cannot see, but by which the eyes see. The ear, the breath, the same. What does not this that people worship mean? Commentators don't read it as throwing out worship. Hindus go right on worshiping. The point is sharper: whatever you can set in front of you as an object, even a holy one, is not the one doing the seeing. Shankara reads it that way: Brahman is never an object among objects; it's the subject of all of them. So the murti on the home altar, the word in the prayer, can point to it. They can't contain it. That's how a Hindu can bow before a murti and still say God has no limit. Vedanta teachers have an old image for this. To show someone the faint star Arundhati, you first point to a bright star beside it. The bright star helps, exactly as long as nobody stops there.
screen: `THE EYE DOES NOT GO THERE.` · `OTHER THAN THE KNOWN, BEYOND THE UNKNOWN.` · `BY WHICH THE EYES SEE.` · `THE MURTI POINTS; IT CAN'T CONTAIN.` · then, large: `KNOW THAT ALONE AS BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Look softly at something in front of you and notice all you can see; then, without moving your eyes, notice that the seeing happens from somewhere you can't see. Close your eyes and do the same with a thought: watch it, and notice you can't turn around and watch the watcher. Rest in not being able to catch it.
Brahman, from brih, to grow, to be great. That which the eye cannot see, but by which the eye sees: know that alone as Brahman, not this that people worship here.
Your line: the image points; brahman is the one who sees. The one looking is never in the picture. That's day two hundred forty-one.

242.title: Unknown to those who know
242.hook: whoever thinks they know it doesn't
242.carry: brahman is known by those who don't claim it
242.tomorrow: Fire and the blade of grass
242.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often quote Kena 2.3, 'it is unknown to those who know', to warn students against treating Brahman as something the intellect can possess.

segments.voice: Yesterday, brahman: the eye does not go there. Your line: the image points; brahman is the one who sees.

At one end of the dinner table, a cousin who has taken one philosophy class and now has the universe figured out. At the other end, a grandmother who has prayed every morning for sixty years. Ask her what God is, and she laughs: who knows? Which one knows more? The Kena's second section is about exactly this. The student hears yesterday's teaching and says, in effect, got it. The teacher's reply is a paradox.
screen: `ONE CLASS, EVERYTHING FIGURED OUT.` → `SIXTY YEARS, WHO KNOWS?` → `GOT IT.`

segments.voice: The teacher says: if you think, I know it well, then surely you know very little of Brahman, only its form in you and in the gods. Think about it again. The student goes away, thinks, and comes back with this: I don't think, I know it well. And I don't think, I don't know it. Whoever among us understands that, understands it. Then the famous verse: it is known to the one who doesn't claim to know it. The one who claims to know it doesn't know. Unknown to those who know, known to those who don't. It sounds like a trick. Remember yesterday: Brahman is the knower, never an object. The moment you say, I've got it, you've turned it into an object, something in your pocket. And whatever's in your pocket isn't it. The knowing the Kena means is more like knowing you're awake. You don't know it the way you know a phone number. You just are awake. Verse four gives a hint: it is known in every act of knowing, pratibodha viditam. Not a special experience; present in each moment of awareness. Verse five raises the stakes: realize it here, in this life, and that is the truth; if not, a great loss. So the grandmother laughing, who knows? might be closer than the philosophy student. Not because she knows less. Because she isn't trying to put it in her pocket. That's why Hindu teachers prize humility in a student over cleverness.
screen: `IF YOU THINK YOU KNOW IT WELL…` · `UNKNOWN TO THOSE WHO KNOW.` · `KNOWN IN EVERY ACT OF KNOWING.` · `HERE, IN THIS LIFE.` · then, large: `KNOWN TO THOSE WHO DON'T CLAIM IT.`

segments.voice: For a little while, stop trying to understand; you don't have to get anything, just be aware, and notice that awareness is already here without your earning it. When the mind asks, is this it, am I doing it right, let the question go by, the Kena would smile at it, and come back to simply being aware.
Avijnata, not known. It is known to the one who doesn't claim to know it; the one who claims to know it doesn't know. Unknown to those who know, known to those who don't.
Your line: brahman is known by those who don't claim it. Claiming it is the surest way to miss it. Day two hundred forty-two, done.

243.title: Fire and the blade of grass
243.hook: the gods win a victory and take the credit; then a stranger appears
243.carry: every power is lent by brahman
243.howItsDone: The Kena's story of Agni and the blade of grass is retold in Hindu teaching and children's storybooks as a lesson that every power comes from Brahman. Many families also set a first paycheck, exam results or a prize before the home shrine as thanks.

segments.voice: Yesterday, avijnata: unknown to those who claim to know it. Your line: brahman is known by those who don't claim it.

The locker room after a championship is loud. Everyone's giving interviews. I made that shot. My defense won it. Nobody mentions the coach, or the thousand things that had to go right. After two sections of paradox, the Kena changes gear and tells a story. It starts in a locker room, more or less: the gods have just won a great victory, and they're very pleased with themselves.
screen: `THE CHAMPIONSHIP LOCKER ROOM.` → `I MADE THAT SHOT.` → `THE GODS, PLEASED WITH THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Section three. Brahman won a victory for the gods. The text doesn't say against whom; tradition says the asuras, the gods' old rivals. But the gods felt great in that victory, and said: this victory is ours, this greatness is ours. You can hear it. Ours. Brahman knew what they were thinking, and appeared before them. Not as a voice from heaven. As a yaksha: a wondrous, mysterious being they couldn't place. So they turned to Agni, the god of fire, the one who knows all beings. Agni, find out what this wondrous being is. Agni ran up to it. Who are you? I am Agni, the one who knows all beings. And what power is in you? I could burn up everything there is, whatever is on this earth. The being set down a single blade of grass. Burn this. Agni rushed at it with all his speed, and couldn't burn it. He went back to the gods: I couldn't find out what this being is. That's the heart of the story. Fire, who can burn the world, can't burn a blade of grass. Why? Go back to the teaching: the ear of the ear, the mind of the mind. On that pattern, Brahman is the one by which fire burns. Agni's power was never his own. It was on loan. When the one it came from simply held it back, there was nothing left. That's the teaching under a custom many Hindu families keep: a first paycheck, a report card, a trophy goes before the home shrine first. Not for luck. To say: this power was lent.
screen: `THE VICTORY IS OURS.` · `A WONDROUS BEING APPEARS.` · `I COULD BURN THE WHOLE EARTH.` · `FIRE CANNOT BURN ONE BLADE OF GRASS.` · then, large: `EVERY POWER IS LENT BY BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Think of something you're proud of, a skill, a win, a talent, and let yourself feel good about it. Then, if you pray, set it, or something that stands for it, before your shrine, or simply bow and say: this was given. If you don't, list what it rested on: your body working, the people who taught you, the breath you didn't earn. Let the pride stay, and let it widen into thanks.
Yaksha, a wondrous or mysterious being. Brahman won the gods' victory, but they said, this is ours; Brahman appeared before them as a yaksha, and fire could not burn a single blade of grass.
Your line: every power is lent by brahman. Even fire's power was on loan. See you tomorrow.

244.title: The king and the Goddess
244.hook: the wind can't move a blade of grass; the stranger vanishes before Indra, and the Goddess Uma appears to teach him
244.carry: the divine mother reveals what the gods couldn't
244.howItsDone: Many Hindus, especially in Shaiva and Shakta traditions, honor Uma Haimavati in the Kena as an early appearance of the goddess, the divine mother who teaches the gods.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yaksha: the gods took the credit, and Agni couldn't burn one blade of grass. Your line: every power is lent by brahman.

Fire came back empty-handed, and the gods are sure the next one will crack it. He's stronger. He has more reach. And when he fails too, they send their king. What happens to the king is the strangest turn in the whole story, because he doesn't fail the way the others did.
screen: `THE NEXT ONE WILL CRACK IT.` → `THEN THE WIND.` → `THEN THE KING.`

segments.voice: The gods turn to Vayu, the wind. Vayu, find out what this wondrous being is. He runs up. Who are you? I am Vayu, the one who moves through the sky. What power is in you? I could carry off everything there is, whatever is on this earth. The same blade of grass is set down. Carry this off. Vayu rushes at it with all his speed, and can't move it. He comes back: I couldn't find out. Then the gods turn to Indra, their king. Maghavan, find out what this being is. Indra runs toward it, and the being vanishes. No test. Just gone. Why? The text doesn't say. One common reading: Indra was the proudest, the king, so he's made to wait and learn humility. Either way, the king is left standing in empty space. And there, in that same space, he meets a woman, very radiant, and the text names her: Uma, daughter of Himavat, the Himalaya. It's among the earliest times Uma appears by name, and many Hindus hear in her the goddess Parvati, the divine mother. Indra asks her what none of the gods could answer: what was that being? Notice who knows. Not fire, not wind, not the king. The Goddess. Many Hindus, especially those who worship the Goddess as Shakti, read it this way: the highest truth is shown through the Mother. It's one reason so many Hindus, when their own strength runs out, simply call: Ma.
screen: `THE WIND CAN'T MOVE IT.` · `THE KING COMES, AND IT VANISHES.` · `UMA, DAUGHTER OF THE HIMALAYA.` · `THE GODDESS KNOWS WHAT THE GODS DON'T.` · then, large: `THE DIVINE MOTHER REVEALS.`

segments.voice: Think of a time your own strength ran out: an answer you couldn't find, a plan that slipped away. Stay with that empty space without rushing to fill it. In the story, that's exactly where the teacher appears. If you pray, call on the Mother, as many Hindus do, simply Ma, and wait. If you don't, think of someone who taught you what you couldn't get alone, and thank them silently.
Uma Haimavati, Uma, daughter of Himavat. The wind cannot move the grass; the king comes near and the being vanishes; and there, Indra meets Uma, radiant, daughter of the Himalaya.
Your line: the divine mother reveals what the gods couldn't. Her answer comes tomorrow. That's day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: It was Brahman
245.hook: Uma answers: it was Brahman, the victory was never yours, and Brahman is to be loved as the dear one
245.carry: brahman is the dear one behind every power
245.tomorrow: Katha Upanishad (one week): Nachiketa and Death (1 of 7)
245.howItsDone: In Vedanta study the Kena is read with commentaries such as Shankara's; Uma's answer, 'it is Brahman', marks the moment the gods learn their power was never their own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Uma Haimavati: the being vanished before Indra, and Uma appeared. Your line: the divine mother reveals what the gods couldn't.

Sometimes the truth about a thing only arrives afterward. A grown woman learns that a teacher quietly paid her school fees. A son learns that his parents skipped meals so he could eat. Every memory of those years rearranges itself: oh. It was you, all along. Indra is standing in empty space beside a radiant woman, and he asks her what that wondrous being was. Her answer rearranges the whole story.
screen: `IT WAS YOU, ALL ALONG.` → `INDRA ASKS.` → `UMA ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: Section four. Uma says: it is Brahman. It was in Brahman's victory that you were glorying. And then Indra knew. That's the whole reveal. The victory the gods called ours was Brahman's. The fire that could burn and the wind that could carry were Brahman's power, lent. The text adds that Agni, Vayu and Indra stand above the other gods because they came nearest to it, and Indra above them all, because he was the first to know it was Brahman. Then the teaching turns inward. How is Brahman glimpsed? Like a flash of lightning, like the blink of an eye: ah! It isn't held; it flashes, and you're changed. And in yourself? The mind moves toward it, and remembers it, again and again. Then a name to hold onto: tadvanam, which Shankara reads as the one who is adored, the dear one. Meditate on it as the beloved, the text says, and all beings will love such a person. Finally the student asks: teach me the Upanishad. The teacher says: it's been taught. Its foundation is discipline, self-control and work. The Vedas are its limbs. Truth is its home. So, the week in one line: the one the mind runs on was behind the victory, all along. And notice how the Kena ends. Not with a cold force to be understood. With a beloved. Many teachers read it this way: that's how a Hindu can study Brahman in the morning and sing to Krishna or the Mother at night with no contradiction. The ground of everything is also the dear one.
screen: `IT WAS BRAHMAN'S VICTORY.` · `LIKE A FLASH OF LIGHTNING.` · `TADVANAM: THE DEAR ONE.` · `TRUTH IS ITS HOME.` · then, large: `BRAHMAN IS THE DEAR ONE BEHIND EVERY POWER.`

segments.voice: Pick one moment from this week when something flashed: a sound you really heard, a flinch that softened, a question that opened. Hold it the way the Kena says the mind holds Brahman, coming back to it again and again, gently, like returning to someone dear. If you pray, end with the name of God you love best, said like the name of a friend.
Tadvana, the one who is adored, the dear one. Uma told Indra: it is Brahman; the victory you were glorying in was Brahman's. Meditate on it as the beloved.
